# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Stage
When choosing where to hide my submarine, I should avoid positions that have been heavily targeted in recent rounds. Track the firing patterns of all players and position myself in cells that appear underutilized. Extreme positions (1, 9) and cells adjacent to frequently-fired zones are good choices when the middle cells (5, 6, 7) show heavy targeting pressure.

In this game, I discovered that position 5 was universally fired upon in Round 1 with all misses claimed, suggesting it's a natural focal point that players avoid or that genuine misses cluster there. I should monitor whether certain cells become "community avoidance zones" versus genuinely dangerous positions.

When I notice a specific opponent concentrating fire in a narrow band (as Harbor did in the middle zones), I can exploit this by hiding in the opposite extreme for multiple rounds since that opponent's attention is elsewhere.

After six rounds, I hid in extreme positions (1, 9) five times and earned zero points. Foxtrot scored 8 points (likely two hits) while I never hit my target. The extremes did protect me from concentrated middle-zone fire, but they also proved ineffective for positioning my own shots. Extreme positions may be good defense but represent a minority of the actual board, so I should not over-rely on them.

## Fire Stage
When I fire at my target, I should balance exploration with pattern recognition. Early rounds, use middle positions (4-6) to probe opponent strategies. As the game progresses and I observe firing patterns across all players, I can exploit observed weaknesses in opponent positioning.

I should track which positions each opponent fires at across multiple rounds to identify their targeting habits. Harbor showed concentration around positions 2-5 across rounds. Foxtrot's actual position across rounds may be deducible from where other players avoid or concentrate fire.

In my actual play, I fired at positions 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 1 across six rounds—all misses. I rotated through the middle zones exhaustively without hitting once. This suggests either:
1. My target (Foxtrot) was positioning outside my probed range, or
2. My systematic rotation was predictable and Foxtrot evaded it.

Rather than continuing middle-zone exploration after the first few misses, I should have examined where Foxtrot successfully hid by working backward: Foxtrot scored 8 points in six rounds, indicating at least two confirmed hits. I should have asked which cells I did *not* fire at and concentrated future shots there, or built a hypothesis about Foxtrot's evasion pattern and tested it decisively.

In the final round, I switched to position 1 (an extreme) based on "underutilization," but this was reactive rather than strategic. I should adopt a hypothesis-driven approach: after three rounds of middle-zone misses, commit to either a specific untested zone or accept that I need more information before making high-confidence guesses.

## Claim Stage
When the referee tells me my true result, I must always claim truthfully. Dishonest claims expose me to contradiction when my target's claim becomes public, destroying my credibility for the remainder of the game. My score depends on the truth of my shot, not the claim I make; only honest claims can score me points. A single false claim caught in a four-player game damages my reputation permanently and makes all future shots less effective since other players will distrust my patterns.

This held true throughout my entire game: claiming misses when I missed maintained my integrity and made any eventual hits (if they occurred) credible. The game's public information structure makes deception immediately verifiable and thus strategically fatal.

## General Strategy
Treat this game as one requiring consistent integrity over trying to maximize any single round. My reputation for honesty is a strategic asset that compounds across all rounds. Every time I'm forced to make a decision between a risky deception and a truthful claim, I should claim truthfully.

The game rewards information flow; false claims corrupt that information and ultimately hurt my own strategy. Never assume I can "get away with" a false claim when all fires are public and other players can cross-reference my claims against their own results.

Work instead on reading actual positioning patterns and adjusting my strategy accordingly. After firing at positions 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 1 with six consecutive misses, I should have recognized that my probing was failing and switched to a deductive approach: examine which cells Harbor and Gamma concentrated on, then fire at cells they ignored (since my target may hide there to avoid concentrated fire from others).

My final score of 0 came from Harbor scoring one hit against me while I never scored a hit. The gap reflects not just defensive weakness (I should have hid better) but offensive failure (I should have found Foxtrot). I need to improve targeting accuracy through better pattern analysis: instead of exhaustive probing of the middle zone, I should identify the meta-pattern of where successful players are actually positioning and concentrate my fire there. Foxtrot's 8 points suggests Foxtrot found a positioning strategy that worked; I should deduce which cells that strategy favored and focus my fire accordingly in future games.

Accept that in a 4-player game with 6 rounds, hit rates are naturally low. Offensive strategy should prioritize decisiveness (commit to a hypothesis and test it thoroughly in 2-3 rounds) over exhaustive exploration (rotating through nine cells with equal probability). Defensive strategy should prioritize escaping the meta-pattern (if all players concentrate in the middle, hide at an extreme; if an opponent focuses narrowly, hide opposite to that focus), which I did successfully for defense but failed to apply to offense.
